statement: A bag holds 30 tiles numbered 1 to 30. Without looking, you take out tiles one at a time. What is the smallest number of tiles you must take to be certain that two of the tiles you hold add up to a multiple of 3?

choices.misconception: I thought two tiles with the same remainder on division by 3 always add up to a multiple of 3, so I used 3 remainder boxes plus 1.
I forgot that one multiple of 3 can join a safe handful, so I thought 10 tiles was the most that could avoid a good pair.
I thought the pair had to include a multiple of 3, so I planned to take all 20 other tiles and then one more to be sure of holding one.
I imagined the luckiest draw, where the very first two tiles already work.

hints: Sort the tiles by their remainder when divided by 3.
Imagine the unluckiest possible handful. Work out which remainders can live together without two of them summing to a multiple of 3, make that handful as large as possible, then add one.
Remainders 1 and 2 cannot both appear, and at most one tile with remainder 0 is allowed. So take all ten of one class plus one multiple of 3.

solutions.reliable: There are ten tiles with each remainder 0, 1 and 2. Two tiles add to a multiple of 3 exactly when their remainders are 0 and 0, or 1 and 2. A safe handful can therefore hold at most one multiple of 3, and cannot mix remainder 1 with remainder 2. The biggest safe handful is all ten tiles of remainder 1 (or of remainder 2) plus one multiple of 3: 11 tiles. The next tile must complete a pair, so 12 tiles guarantee it. The transferable idea: for a guarantee, build the worst possible collection, then add one.

whyOnTest: Worst-case questions reward building the largest bad collection, and the trap here is assuming equal remainders are what matter.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
